content.title: When will DISH blackout end? What to watch instead, free streaming comparisons
content.text: Here's your complete guide to surviving the DISH channel blackout using these free trials and live streaming deals. Photo credit: David Becker/Getty ImagesDavid Becker/Getty ImagesIf you purchase a product through a link on our site, we may receive compensation.Millions of DISH Network subscribers across the U.S. continue to experience a widespread blackout that began March 10 after contract negotiations between DISH Network and Gray Media collapsed.The dispute has resulted in 226 local broadcast stations across 113 markets being removed from DISH’s satellite TV lineup, affecting access to major network affiliates including ABC, CBS, FOX, NBC, CW, MyNetworkTV and Telemundo. The blackout has disrupted access to local news, severe weather alerts, live sports and primetime TV — leaving many households scrambling for alternative ways to watch.How to still watch ABC, CBS, FOX, NBC and moreThankfully, there are several reliable, cost-effective workarounds. Below are the best ways to keep watching impacted channels.Stream network programming on these appsDirect‑to‑consumer (DTC) apps continue to offer live or next‑day programming for most major networks:ABC: DIRECTV, Fubo, SlingNBC: Peacock, DIRECTV, SlingCBS: Paramount+, Fubo, DIRECTV, SlingFOX: Fubo, DIRECTV, SlingTelemundo: Peacock, DIRECTV, SlingCW: Fubo, DIRECTVSwitch to a live TV streaming serviceIf you want full access to live local channels, several streaming services currently carry ABC, CBS, FOX and NBC in most markets. Details include:FuboFree trial and up to $30 off first month203–294+ channels, including many local affiliatesStrong sports lineupDIRECTVFive‑day free trial and up to $40 off first month90–185+ channels depending on planAll major networks available in most marketsSling TV50% off first monthCarries FOX & NBC in select markets (Blue plan)Low‑cost and customizable streaming passesPeacockAffordable plans from $7.99/moStreams NBC content, live sports, plus originalsParamount+Limited-time two months for $2.99/mo for all plansStreams CBS live (on Premium plan)Includes SHOWTIMEHow long will the blackout last?As of March 19, no end date has been announced, with negotiations at a standstill and both sides trading blame.Industry analysts note that past Gray disputes were resolved within days, but the current standoff appears more entrenched due to the unprecedented terms each side claims the other proposed.Neither DISH nor Gray has filed an FCC complaint yet, though it remains a possibility if talks fail to progress. Both companies publicly state they are willing to resume negotiations, but no breakthroughs have been reported since the blackout began.Why the DISH–Gray Media dispute escalatedAt the heart of the dispute are retransmission consent fees, which pay‑TV providers like DISH pay to local station owners like Gray Media.DISH’s positionDISH claims Gray Media demanded steep, above‑market fee increases during renewal talks, despite declining traditional TV viewership and the rise of free or low‑cost alternatives. According to DISH, Gray also introduced last‑minute conditions involving stations it did not yet own, which stalled negotiations just hours before the contract expired. DISH says it refused the increases to avoid raising monthly bills for subscribers. Gray Media’s positionGray Media, meanwhile, accuses DISH of demanding a “materially adverse” and unprecedented contract provision not found in any of its 400 other distribution agreements. Gray claims DISH violated its legal obligation to negotiate in good faith under FCC rules.Gray has acknowledged that DISH dropped its stations but has not provided detailed public comment on the disputed fee increases.What to expect going forwardCarriage disputes like this one have become increasingly common across the TV landscape as broadcasters seek higher fees while providers resist passing costs on to subscribers. Analysts warn that if the standoff continues:DISH may face permanent subscriber losses to streaming competitors.Gray Media risks lower advertising reach since millions of viewers currently cannot watch their stations.While rapid resolutions have occurred in past Gray‑related disputes, the unprecedented contract terms each side alleges here appear to be prolonging negotiations beyond what viewers typically experience.
